claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.

A Helm chart is a directory of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata; the `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi (the pulumi/pulumi repository) is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Pulumi supports general-purpose languages (with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management), plus YAML and HCL, for authoring infrastructure.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm applies resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind, defined in the Helm source file pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go.
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK available in every supported Pulumi language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with rules written in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management, and the Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.

Helm docs (https://helm.sh/docs/topics/charts/#operational-aspects-of-using-dependencies) state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source, beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs its kind-ordered resource list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the Kubernetes API server in a single pass and does not wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Helm chart dependencies do not change resource ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else, so a chart cannot express installing a database subchart before an application subchart or starting a Deployment after a Job completes.
The workaround for ordering in Helm is chart hooks ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, and resources created by hooks are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph that determines operation order.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi's dependency-graph ordering with parallel deployment of independent resources makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi deletes resources following the same dependency graph in reverse.

`helm.v4.Chart` in the Pulumi Kubernetes provider supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and `helm rollback` restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and users roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release, while Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare; Helm manages Kubernetes resources only.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns (orchestrating a production-ready cluster end-to-end, and wiring Pulumi outputs into chart values) cover most production deployments that use Pulumi and Helm together.

A single Pulumi program can create the cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide (/docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/) walks through the pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack via Helm charts end-to-end.

Resource outputs from elsewhere in a Pulumi program (such as an `aws.rds.Instance` connection string, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, or a Cloudflare zone ID) flow into a Helm chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs; Pulumi resolves the values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
The FAQ heading "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" exists on this page at anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, and they can be combined.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern for adopting Pulumi alongside Helm.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with `helm template` and converting the resulting YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring existing in-cluster resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding code.

The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`, and a Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private) and pass values as typed Pulumi inputs, including outputs from other resources.

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency does not make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.
The page contains a section headed "Resource ordering and dependencies" (anchor #resource-ordering-and-dependencies) that details how Pulumi orders resources by their actual dependencies.

The page contains a section "Adoption: coexistence, conversion, and import" at anchor #adoption-coexistence-conversion-and-import covering keeping upstream charts in Pulumi or converting charts to native Pulumi code.
